justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward bias from what I'd assume was a recent reference price near 3,100 on the S&P 500. At the one-day horizon, I anchored closely to that level, adding a small positive drift consistent with the historical tendency for equities to drift slightly higher on any given day. At the one-week horizon, I maintained a similarly modest upward tilt, reflecting the idea that near-term macro conditions were neither dramatically bullish nor bearish, suggesting mean-reverting behavior around recent trading ranges. For the one-month estimate, I projected a slightly higher level, incorporating the long-run equity risk premium and assuming no major regime change, while acknowledging that monthly moves tend to be dominated by news flow rather than simple drift.

The confidence interval widths reflect the well-known scaling of volatility with the square root of time. At the one-day horizon, realized S&P 500 volatility of roughly 15–18% annualized implies daily moves of about 1%, so a 90% interval spanning roughly plus or minus 70 points seemed appropriate. At the one-week horizon, uncertainty compounds, widening the band to about 270 points in total. By one month, the interval opens further to roughly 540 points, reflecting that monthly realized volatility historically produces moves of 4–6% in either direction under normal conditions, and considerably more during stress periods.

Specific risks that could push outcomes outside my stated intervals include a sudden deterioration in credit markets or a banking stress event, which historically produces gap moves well beyond one standard deviation. A significant surprise in Federal Reserve communications — such as an emergency rate change or an unexpected pivot in forward guidance — could similarly cause a rapid repricing. On the upside, an unexpected resolution of geopolitical tensions or a surprisingly strong earnings season could propel the index above the upper bound of my one-month interval.

Finally, I want to be transparent that these estimates carry model uncertainty on top of market uncertainty. My intervals assume something close to a log-normal return distribution with roughly stationary volatility, but actual equity returns have fat tails and volatility clustering. If we are near a volatility regime shift — for instance, if implied volatility were already elevated when I made this forecast — the true intervals should be meaningfully wider than what I stated, particularly at the one-month horizon where tail events have more time to materialize.
